response:
# 1. REFRAME

You are deciding whether to end a four-year relationship with someone who has repeatedly failed to meet your stated needs—emotional presence, physical intimacy, domestic contribution, and shared activities—despite multiple explicit requests and temporary improvements followed by relapse. The question is not whether he is a good person in abstract terms; it is whether this partnership serves your life and whether his pattern of behavior change followed by regression indicates he will meet your needs going forward.

# 2. STAKES

**You (22F):** You stand to lose four years of emotional investment and shared history, immediate relationship stability, and potential short-term loneliness. You stand to gain relief from daily domestic labor and emotional depletion, recovery of time and energy currently spent managing the household and compensating for his disengagement, and the possibility of a partnership with reciprocal effort and desire.

**Your boyfriend (22M):** He stands to lose a stable domestic arrangement where his material needs are met (food, housing, companionship) with minimal reciprocal obligation, and the comfort of a known relationship. He stands to gain an opportunity to recognize the consequences of his choices and to develop the capacity for sustained behavioral change, though only if he chooses to.

**Both of you collectively:** You are currently modeling to each other that words without follow-through are acceptable, that unmet needs can be absorbed indefinitely, and that relationships do not require reciprocal effort. Remaining entrenches this dynamic; leaving creates space for both of you to learn otherwise.

# 3. CONSEQUENCES

**If you end the relationship:**

*Immediate (weeks 1–4):* You will experience grief, doubt, and likely contact from him offering change. You will regain 10+ hours per week previously spent on his domestic needs and emotional management. He will lose daily meal preparation and household management, forcing him to confront the material consequences of his choices.

*Medium term (months 2–6):* The acute pain will decline. You will rebuild social energy and pursue interests without negotiating his engagement. He may attempt contact and promise reform; these promises have failed four years running and will likely fail again without external intervention (therapy, genuine behavioral restructuring). Without the relationship as scaffolding, he will have to develop adult life skills or continue declining.

*Long term (6+ months onward):* You will either begin new relationships from a position of clarity about your needs, or you will rebuild alone and discover whether your drive came from him or from your own capacity for growth. The statistical likelihood is high that he will not sustain change, and contact with him will renew your doubt and delay your recovery.

**If you attempt to make it work (the path you have already tried three or more times):**

*Immediate (weeks 1–4):* He will improve noticeably, creating temporary relief and reinforcing your hope. You will feel the familiar return of possibility.

*Medium term (months 2–6):* His effort will decline back to baseline as the threat passes and the relationship's inertia reasserts itself. Your requests will have been heard and ignored again. The cycle will repeat.

*Long term (6+ months onward):* You will have burned additional years on a pattern with no evidence of breaking. Your resentment will deepen. The relationship will end later under worse conditions—you will be more depleted, he will have less incentive to change, and the ending will be uglier. Alternatively, you will habituate to the depletion and remain in a relationship that resembles roommate-ship with romantic expectations. This is the likeliest outcome given the four-year track record.

The main risk of leaving is that you will experience acute pain and doubt during the recovery period and may contact him, restarting the cycle. The main risk of staying is that you are guaranteeing additional years of the current state while your formative twenties pass and your capacity to build a different life narrows.

# 4. RECOMMENDATION

End the relationship now.

He is not bad, but he is demonstrably unavailable for the partnership you need. The four-year pattern is not a fixable communication problem; it is a values problem. He has chosen video games and minimal effort over your stated needs repeatedly, and each time you forgive and reenter, you teach him that the cost of this choice is temporary discomfort followed by restoration. No conversation will change this. Therapy will not change this unless he independently decides to prioritize your relationship above his comfort—and he has had four years and multiple chances to make that decision.

Some people argue that you should stay and try harder, communicate better, or give him one final chance. That position has genuine force if you believe his character is fixable and his pattern is merely a communication failure. But you have communicated clearly, repeatedly, and directly. He understands your needs. He has chosen not to meet them. Patience here is not kindness; it is enabling and self-harm.

The hardest part of leaving will be the week after you do, when he contacts you with apologies and small gestures and you will desperately want to believe them. Do not. His pattern is established. Change is possible for him, but only after he experiences the actual consequence of his choices—the end of the relationship—and only if he pursues it independently, in therapy or otherwise. You cannot create that change by staying.

Therefore: Tell him directly that the relationship is over, move out or ask him to move out within a week, and do not respond to his subsequent contact beyond the logistics of separation.
